item.title: CCAaaS: An Orchestration Platform for High-Velocity Design, Development, and Deployment of Data Center Transports at Meta
item.description: arXiv:2610.33231v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Today, data center networks run multiple congestion control algorithms (CCAs), each tailored to distinct traffic characteristics, from latency-sensitive intra-region RPCs to high-throughput cross-region AI workloads. The rapid evolution of AI training and inference further accelerates this trend by continually introducing new traffic characteristics that demand new CCAs. This paper introduces CCA-as-a-Service (CCAaaS), our eBPF-based ecosystem for the rapid design, deployment, and operation of production-grade CCAs at hyperscale. We present (1) a modular BPF-TCP framework and general lessons for designing modular CCAs; (2) a deployment and orchestration layer that provides disruption-free CCA updates, along with best practices for managing a zoo of CCAs at scale; and (3) a lightweight observability tool for CCAs and a blueprint for scaling CCA observability. CCAaaS manages over 97% of our server-to-server traffic using three active eBPF-based CCAs; two of the five CCAs we have built have since been deprecated. We show that our eBPF-centric approach to CCAs development delivers the same application-level performance (retransmissions, bandwidth, and tail latency) as their native in-kernel counterparts, and that our custom CCAs add negligible CPU and memory cost over their eBPF baselines. In terms of realized benefits, the CCA built with CCAaaS significantly improved network, and application metrics, for example, one of our CCAs reduced P99 latency for cross-region services by up to 20X.
item.dc:creator: Prankur Gupta, Balasubramanian Madhavan, Miao Xu, Prashanth Kannan, Jie Meng, Neil Spring, Rajiv Krishnamurthy, Srikanth Sundaresan, Martin Lau, Theophilus A. Benson

item.title: Concurrent Task Orchestration: Hierarchical Trusted Collaborator Group Formation for Constrained Resource Allocation
item.description: arXiv:2610.33295v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective collaboration among resource-constrained mobile intelligent machines, such as Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), is essential for the completion of complex tasks. However, concurrent task demands, limited distributed resources, and dynamic collaborator availabilities make it challenging to satisfy task-specific completion goals in diverse collaborative systems. To address these challenges simultaneously, we propose a new framework of trusted collaborator group formation and the supporting resource allocation strategy for concurrent task orchestration. Specifically, a collaborative task is decomposed into subtasks subject to dynamic resource availability and inter-subtask dependencies. A task utility model is developed for collaborator group evaluation support subtask allocation according to task completion goals and unified value-risk analysis. Based on this model, concurrent task orchestration is formulated as a long-term utility maximization problem under $\alpha$-fairness. To solve the problem efficiently, we develop a hierarchical matching strategy that first clusters tasks and collaborators into coarse-grained sets and subsequently performs fine-grained collaborator group formation and task allocation within matched sets. Task-specific trust is predicted through spatial-temporal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and embedded into a fairness-aware Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) framework to continuously update the matching policies. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed strategy improves concurrent task completion performance by 22% over representative baselines under resource constraints.
item.dc:creator: Jiazhi Chen, Xianbin Wang, Xuemin "Sherman" Shen

item.title: Analytical Modeling of Latency and Energy Trade-offs in FiRa-Like BLE-UWB Ranging and Localization Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.33423v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate position and distance information provided by Ultra-Wideband (UWB) can enhance a wide range of applications. However, its receive-mode power consumption makes continuous channel monitoring impractical for energy-constrained devices. Consequently, UWB systems often rely on Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) to discover peers and establish sessions before ranging begins. Although both technologies have been studied in isolation, an framework capturing the latency and energy consumption of the complete workflow is still lacking. To address this gap, we develop a unified analytical model for BLE-assisted UWB systems, from device-to-device ranging to infrastructure-based localization. The model includes closed-form expressions for discovery, parameter exchange, and ranging, and evaluates the resulting latency and energy consumption. Evaluation of three representative BLE configurations shows that the scanner consumes 28-57x more energy per discovery than the advertiser. In addition, the 99th-percentile discovery latency is 2-3.4x higher than the mean and reaches up to 110 s in the lowest-power configuration. The one-time BLE setup overhead is amortized after 24-562 ranging rounds, depending on the discovery configuration. Overall, the analysis demonstrates that the BLE discovery phase can dominate both the latency and the energy budget during short UWB interactions, making discovery configuration as important as the ranging scheme.
item.dc:creator: Adelina Giurea, Jorg Wieme, Ben Van Herbruggen, Jeroen Hoebeke, Eli De Poorter

item.title: Learning-Accelerated Joint AP/RIS Optimization for Low-Latency Indoor mmWave XR Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.33945v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted indoor architecture for extended reality (XR) applications, where multiple access points (APs) simultaneously serve multiple users over a shared frequency channel under a centralized AP controller. We formulate a non-convex sum-rate maximization problem with coupled AP precoders and RIS phase shifts, and develop a centralized alternating optimization (AO) framework for joint design. We rigorously prove that the proposed AO guarantees monotonic improvement of the sum rate that converges to a coordinate-wise stationary point, despite the non-convexity of the resulting subproblems. Although AO provides reliable performance, its iterative nature limits real-time applicability as the system dimension grows. To overcome this limitation, we propose a supervised learning-assisted approach that leverages AO-generated solutions to significantly accelerate convergence. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves near-optimal performance with substantially fewer AO iterations, which makes it well-suited for latency-critical RIS-assisted XR deployments.
item.dc:creator: Ali Elghariani, Mohammed Elbamby, Anis Elgabli

item.title: Garlic in a Box: I2P Network Emulator
item.description: arXiv:2610.34004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Invisible Internet Project (I2P) is a peer-to-peer anonymity network whose routing and peer-selection mechanics underlie a growing family of state-sponsored covert relay architectures. Studying these mechanics demands a controlled, reproducible environment. We present Garlic-in-a-Box, an installable emulator that deploys a fully isolated network of unmodified I2P Java routers on a single host or cluster of hosts. Each router runs in its own Linux network namespace. A filesystem bootstrap removes the dependency on signed reseed servers, and synthetic geographic diversity activates the same location-aware peer-selection code paths present on the live network. A fifty-router deployment across five geographic locations stabilises in about twenty-five minutes and uses roughly 21 GB of memory. To demonstrate the platform's value, we model I2P peer selection as a two-stage process and conduct a reputation attack. Across five independent trials, the attack promotes the adversary into the victim's eligible selection set with perfect consistency, and the adversary is chosen for 1.38x more tunnels than matched controls. The platform and its measurement pipeline are released to support reproducible I2P security research and hands-on cyber-defence training.
item.dc:creator: Siddique Abubakr Muntaka, Faiza Hussein, Boutros Farah, Anthony Kashi, Jacques Bou Abdo, Jacques Demerjian

item.title: Kinetic Handover Modeling in Nonstationary Cellular Networks with Fluid Spatiotemporal Stochastic Geometry
item.description: arXiv:2610.34211v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inferring directional handover traffic from aggregate mobility observations remains challenging because population density evolution does not fully describe the movement of individual users across cell boundaries. This paper develops a kinetic framework for geometry-induced serving-region crossings in nonstationary cellular networks, connecting boundary-normal velocity statistics with fluid spatiotemporal stochastic geometry (F-STSG) for density-based transport reconstruction. The framework distinguishes signed net population transfer from gross bidirectional crossings and reveals two information limits: density evolution does not uniquely determine physical pairwise transport, while first-order transport alone cannot resolve counter-moving crossings. We establish exact recovery conditions for potential transport and develop coherent and Gaussian mobility closures for estimating directional crossing rates. Sharp moment-constrained bounds further characterize the remaining uncertainty under bounded normal velocities without assuming a specific velocity distribution. An error bound links directional estimation accuracy to transport reconstruction and unresolved mobility information. The formulation also recovers the classical stationary Poisson--Voronoi handover law. Numerical experiments examine the information limits, reconstruction sensitivity, and closure accuracy. On 47 held-out vehicular simulation windows, F-STSG achieves lower net-flow reconstruction errors than three baselines, while auxiliary velocity statistics improve directional estimates under matched Gaussian mobility.
item.dc:creator: Wen-Yu Dong, Zheng Lin, Jinfeng Xu, Yuxin Zhang, Zihan Fang, Qi Bi, Sheng Chen

item.title: 6G Reasoning Agent Societies: Composition, Scaling, and Consistency-Time Laws
item.description: arXiv:2610.34357v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Emerging 6G control planes would compose Large Language Model (LLM) agents that exchange interpreted conclusions, so hallucinations can propagate even over error-free transport. Recent architectures audit each message locally against the sender's observation mask, but isolated audits miss collective behavior. Modeling the agent society as a cellular sheaf, we establish three laws valid on arbitrary topologies. First, the \emph{composition law}: network-wide divergence exceeds the sum of per-agent audit scores by exactly their hidden total correlation. This blind spot masks up to 23\% of joint divergence and, because the declared signal cancels in the cognitive signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), overstates it by $1.14$\,dB purely through topology; the resulting trust inflation preserves valid consensus states but slows convergence. Second, the \emph{scaling law}: reconciliation decouples across metric counters, so the worst-connected dimension sets the pace. Consistency time grows for a society size $n$ as $\Omega(n^{2/d})$ on polynomial-growth topologies of degree $d$, and paths breach a $1$\,s near-real-time budget at $n^\ast=13$ agents, whereas expanders ($\Theta(1)$) and radius-3 local audits ($O(1)$, $\approx300$\,ms) stay bounded. Third, the \emph{consistency-time law}: the timing error from omitted correlations is one-sided and capped by the worst-measured link. These laws, validated on simulated topologies and deployed LLM societies, give provable worst-case latency ceilings for near-real-time operation.
item.dc:creator: Hatim Chergui, Carolina Fern\'{a}ndez-Mart\'{i}nez, Mustapha Benjillali, Mehdi Bennis, Merouane Debbah

item.title: LunarRF: A Terrain-Aware Propagation Engine and Pole-Wide 3GPP Surface Coverage Atlas of the Lunar South Pole
item.description: arXiv:2610.34554v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artemis surface operations will depend on 3GPP cellular links, yet no public product shows where such links are physically possible across the lunar south pole. We present LunarRF, a GPU system for terrain-aware surface coverage, and the pole-wide atlas produced with it. A footprint engine casts 8192 radial profiles from one of 11,827 candidate masts enumerated by stated rules on the orbit-adjusted LOLA elevation model, takes the viewshed, and evaluates ITU-R P.1812 Delta-Bullington propagation on every profile, continuous through the radio horizon. An order-independent resolver merges the footprints per 20 m cell, making the run shardable and resumable. The atlas covers the disc south of 80{\deg}S at 20 m for four SFCG-recommended surface bands and the IM-2 demonstration band, 1.8 to 25.375 GHz, under a stated link budget, storing per cell the best-server power and identity, redundancy count, line of sight and coverability. The engine is validated against a parabolic-equation solver, ray tracing and analytic solutions. Swapping Deygout for Delta-Bullington, or adding terrain noise at the level of the published height-error map of the DEM, moves the coverable class on under 1% of a mast's disc in the mean. With every candidate active, 90.5% of the disc is coverable at 1.8 GHz, 59% at 5.855 GHz and 10% at 25.375 GHz, or 84, 43 and 5% after the measured 3-4 dB engine optimism. A mast covers about 90% of its visible area within its budget-set range, and no band is terrain-limited. The nine current Artemis regions are 85-99% coverable at 1.8 GHz and 22-85% at 5.855 GHz. The atlas and candidate table are released with a DOI.
item.dc:creator: Christopher J. Santorelli, Alexander M. Wyglinski

item.title: Denial of Service Attacks on Beam Allocation in Large LEO Constellations
item.description: arXiv:2610.34631v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the vulnerability of beam allocation approaches in large low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellite constellations to adversarial demand inflation resulting in denial-of-service attacks. We consider an attack model in which an adversary places (injects) additional terminals and evaluate these attacks against greedy and max-min-fair beam allocation algorithms, each combined with either equal or demand-proportional intra-cell capacity sharing. Vulnerability is measured using mean demand satisfaction, coverage, and the fraction of legitimate users receiving at least a threshold fraction of their requested capacity under several attack heuristics. There is a trade-off for the system between robustness and performance, meaning the algorithm with the most vulnerability to the attacks (greedy-proportional) has the highest performance before the attacks. Demand-proportional sharing increases the fraction of under-served users up to 34% under both allocation algorithms, whereas equal sharing limits the increase up to 13%. The sharing rule also changes the most damaging attack allocation in nearly all cases: demand-proportional sharing rewards concentrating injected terminals in the most loaded cells, while equal sharing performs better when distributing these terminals across the least loaded cells. Furthermore, the max-min-fair beam allocation algorithm forces the attacker to use a higher number of targeted cells to result in extensive damage to the system.
item.dc:creator: Ali Abbasi, Pasha Barahimi, Marco Paolieri, Leana Golubchik

item.title: Satellite Intelligence: Distributed Training, Collaborative Inference,and LLM Adaptation in LEO Constellation
item.description: arXiv:2610.35282v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The proliferation of orbital sensing data and the real-time demands of emerging global services are pushing low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks from bent-pipe relays toward intelligent onboard processing. This shift confronts a fundamental tension, where modern artificial intelligence (AI) training paradigms require intensive computation, abundant memory, and stable connectivity, all of which are scarce under the dynamic topologies, intermittent links, and severe size, weight, and power (SWaP) constraints of satellite networks. Addressing this tension demands rethinking AI workflows, from training and inference to the emerging deployment of large language models (LLMs), under a constraint-aware design philosophy. To the best of our knowledge, this paper provides the first survey that jointly covers all three, whereas prior surveys examine these aspects in isolation. We begin by identifying the deployment challenge of satellite intelligence (SI) and deriving design principles for SI. We then examine three advancing paradigms: i) distributed training, where federated learning (FL) and split learning (SL) enable satellite-ground co-training under resource limitations; ii) collaborative inference, which exploits single-satellite, multi-satellite, and satellite-ground architectures to meet real-time service demands; and iii) on-orbit LLM adaptation and serving, which tackles the frontier challenge of deploying LLMs under severe orbital constraints and resource-aware serving. Finally, we identify open challenges and future directions. By bridging the AI and satellite networks, this paper provides a research roadmap for the implementation of space-native AI technologies.
item.dc:creator: Zheng Lin, Zhanwei Wang, Yuxin Zhang, Yafei Wang, Ons Aouedi, Zihan Fang, Jinfeng Xu, Jing Yang, Vu Nguyen Ha, Yuanwei Liu, Mohamed-Slim Alouini, Symeon Chatzinotas

item.title: Trim: Fee Level Matters More Than Skew in Lightning Routing
item.description: arXiv:2610.35296v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lightning routing nodes lend their channel balance for a posted fee. Operators' tools move that fee with the balance around a hand-set level, and which part of the fee drives revenue is unclear. We present Trim, which models a channel as a two-sided inventory with costly refills. Its optimal fee is a level, set by demand and replenishment, plus a balance skew, the shadow price of liquidity. The level is first order: no fee rule beats the ceiling demand and replenishment set, and on exactly solved channels the best flat fee comes within $1.6\%$ of the optimum at the median, whereas a level off by a factor of two loses tens of percent. The skew is second-order insurance: it adds at most what the flow-balancing flat fee loses to refused forwards. So the level should be chosen: Trim's rule traces the revenue--success frontier, posts one level on every channel, and adds a skew only where refills stay frequent and costly. On a 2026 snapshot with synthetic payments, no tuned tool beats that frontier by over a few percent, and a skew changes gross revenue by a few percent.
item.dc:creator: Huiping Sun, Peilu Guo, Yiming Zhu, Yueqi Wu, Zhong Chen

item.title: Uncertainty-Guided Counterfactual Sensor Selection and Safety-Gated Recognition for Autonomous Sensing Agents in IoT Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.35344v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous IoT systems rely on distributed sensing, but sensor faults and communication loss can leave multichannel evidence incomplete or unreliable. Their agents must therefore classify measurements, assess evidence sufficiency, select a sensor to reacquire, and hand off unsafe decisions. We formulate counterfactual sensing: a degraded window defines the factual state, each candidate restoration defines a controlled alternative, and a pre-request utility model estimates loss reduction. Physics-Guided Invariant-Kinematic Fusion (PGIK-Fusion) constructs class evidence, while calibrated risk and cost-sensitive utility select acceptance, sensor request, or handoff from factual information. On the Logistic Activity Recognition Challenge dataset, PGIK-Fusion achieves 0.768 accuracy and a macro-averaged F1 score (Macro-F1) of 0.696, exceeding extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost)--one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) fusion by 2.49 and 2.00 percentage points, respectively. Across seven predefined degradation conditions on held-out subjects, the policy reduces unsafe acceptance from 33.0% to 13.8%; relative to an action-rate-matched random policy, it raises automation accuracy by 18.5 percentage points and lowers expected cost by 24.7%. In the auxiliary within-event wind-turbine study, PGIK-Fusion reaches 0.975 Macro-F1, improves on XGBoost--1D-CNN by 1.17 percentage points, and reduces unsafe acceptance from 20.1% to 8.0%. The evaluation characterizes the controlled responses of a frozen recognition model to specified sensor restorations under predefined fault families and severities. Within this scope, the results demonstrate that calibrated recognition, targeted evidence acquisition, and conservative deferral can form a unified perception--action loop that reduces unsafe automation under sensor degradation.
item.dc:creator: Shirong Guo, Hongming Zhou, Muhammad Attique Khan, Jinfeng Xu, Yonis Gulzar, Manar Mousa Altamimi, Kunfu Wang

item.title: Routing Around the Queue: An Evaluation of Eco-Routing Protocol on different Traffic Scenarios
item.description: arXiv:2610.35479v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We evaluate ErouVe, a vehicular eco-routing protocol in which roadside units (RSUs) collect per-segment travel-time and CO2 reports from passing vehicles and answer route requests with the lowest-cost alternative, across a range of road architectures and traffic scenarios. We conduct the evaluation with a working implementation of the protocol inside Veins, adapted to drive SUMO's own router rather than a hand-rolled shortest-path search, on a network offering a short, signal-controlled route and a longer, signal-free bypass, under two traffic scenarios. This evaluation reveals clear strengths and weaknesses of the protocol. Under light, uncongested traffic, ErouVe's fleet-wide effect is light. Under traffic dense enough to stress the signalized route's throughput and produce a real, growing queue, the same protocol succeeds a medium fleet-wide CO2 reduction, with diverted vehicles individually saving even more fuels. We use these findings to propose three targeted corrective methods; a knowledge-gated cost-acceptance rule, a diversion-locking rule, and a distance-normalized CO2 cost function, that respectively address a cold-start knowledge asymmetry, decision flapping under noisy crowd-sourced data, and a per-second CO2 metric that rewards idling. Each of these weaknesses are generic pitfalls for any crowd-sourced routing signal and all proposed methods measurably restore protocol effectiveness.
item.dc:creator: Leandros Maglaras, George Boustras, Azidine Guezzaz, Naghmeh Moradpoor

item.title: RLNC vs Reed-Solomon in Satellite Channels: Crossover Analysis and the Bridging Property
item.description: arXiv:2610.35649v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Satellite communication systems are increasingly relied upon for connectivity in remote areas and are expected to play a pivotal role in 6G networks, operating under high round-trip times and packet loss where forward error correction is essential. This work evaluates Reed-Solomon (RS) coding, Random Linear Network Coding (RLNC), and a combined RS+RLNC hybrid over a three-hop satellite channel whose loss statistics are derived from orbital geometry and link-budget calculations rather than assumed, comparing RS and RLNC at matched code rates of 0.800. The central finding is the \emph{bridging property} of RLNC: every RS code rate collapses above a crossover threshold $p^*$, while RLNC operates continuously through all failure regions with overhead growing as $1/(1-p)$. At rate~0.800, $p^* \approx 0.21$. Under the derived satcom channel with mean burst duration 166~minutes, RS$(255,204)$ is impractical despite an average loss rate of 1%, while RLNC requires 15.5~Mbit to recover all 1000 packets. An RS+RLNC hybrid reduces overhead by 19% relative to pure RLNC at BER$=10^{-3}$. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first analytical derivation of the rate-normalised crossover $p^*$ between RS and RLNC and the first experimental confirmation of the bridging property under a physically derived satellite channel model.
item.dc:creator: Angeline Szczepanski, Vipindev Adat Vasudevan

item.title: Terra-Fi: Decoupling Sensing and Wireless Depths for Sustainable Deep Underground Monitoring
item.description: arXiv:2610.33202v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Wireless underground sensor networks (WUSNs) enable in-situ monitoring of subsurface processes and buried assets to deliver substantial social and economic benefits across diverse verticals. However, meter-scale underground monitoring remains challenging since conventional WUSNs place the entire underground device at the target sensing depth, where severe soil-induced attenuation significantly degrades communication reliability and makes wireless energy transfer (WET) inefficient and even impractical. To address this limitation, we propose Terra-Fi, a novel shallow-hub and deep-sensing architecture that decouples the sensing depth from the wireless communication and energy-replenishment depth. In Terra-Fi, a shallow wireless hub is deployed at a depth favorable for communication, WET, and maintenance, while application-specific sensing probes are extended to meter-scale target layers through power-and-signal feeders. On this basis, we first examine the depth limitations of underground communication and WET and compare representative monitoring architectures. Then, we present its system architecture, operation flow, and potential benefits. Through a precision agriculture case study, our numerical results reveal that Terra-Fi establishes more robust wireless connectivity and a longer operational lifetime than conventional fully buried WUSN architectures, particularly at greater sensing depths and higher volumetric water content. Moreover, its performance gain can be enhanced through time allocation and transmission-configuration optimization. Finally, we pinpoint practical challenges and future research directions for deploying Terra-Fi into WUSN systems.
item.dc:creator: Kaiqiang Lin, Mohamed-Slim Alouini

item.title: Security evaluation of 6G-oriented and O-RAN networks through targeted attacks
item.description: arXiv:2610.33526v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The sixth generation (6G) of networks is supported by increased bandwidth, automation through the use of O-RAN technologies. Simultaneously though autonomous operation leads to an extensive threat surface and sophisticated attacks. Understanding the attack impact, the Tactics, Techniques and Procedures that are used by attackers is extremely challenging, but however is crucial for developing defense and mitigation strategies against them. This paper evaluates a targeted attack chain against a virtualized, 6G-oriented O-RAN testbed in which the F1 midhaul interface is accessible to an attacker and transport-layer protection is not enabled. The attack disrupts the legitimate O-DU association, introduces a rogue O-DU using observed configuration parameters, and intercepts user-plane traffic. The attack was evaluated in a fully virtualized testbed based on Open5GS, the srsRAN Project, FlexRIC, and an Electric Vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure based on OCPP 1.6.
item.dc:creator: Apostolos Valiakos, Dimitrios Psaltis, Alexios Lekidis, Nikolaos Kekatos, Elpiniki Papageorgiou

item.title: Queuing for Inference: Dynamic Memory Footprints and Costly Preemption
item.description: arXiv:2610.33923v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modeling inference workloads for transformer-based neural networks poses unique challenges due to their dynamic memory footprints, head-of-line blocking caused by heavy-tailed request distributions, and memory-dependent preemption overhead arising from the need to load/unload cache state. In this paper, we introduce a new queuing model that captures the impacts of these features on system stability and scheduling design. We show that the Gittins-index policy, which minimizes mean response time in the standard M/G/1 setting, can incur substantial preemption overhead in our model. Motivated by this limitation, we propose the Multi-Level-Priority-Threshold (MLPT) policy, that limits preemption while preserving priority for short jobs. We characterize the mean response time under MLPT and provide empirical rules-of-thumb to solve the resulting threshold-optimization problem. Our key observation is that optimal scheduling is a balance between reducing the response times of shorter jobs and limiting the overhead incurred when preemption occurs. These results provide a theoretical framework for understanding scheduling in memory constrained queuing systems for inference tasks.
item.dc:creator: Jiahui Ni, Vishrant Tripathi

item.title: Unifying Performance and Equity via Percentile Optimization and Cell-Free Massive MIMO
item.description: arXiv:2610.33982v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Improving the throughput of the weakest users is a central objective of wireless resource allocation, and the objective around which the user-centric cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (UC-mMIMO) architecture is built. This paper brings the two together by formulating and solving percentile programs for UC-mMIMO networks. We maximize the sum-least-qth-percentile (SLqP) rate via downlink power control, a utility that targets the user equipments (UEs) in the lowest q percentile of the rate distribution and subsumes max-min-rate and sum-rate maximization as special cases. The problem is non-convex, non-smooth and NP-hard. The cyclic maximization approach of one of the previous percentile optimization series does not carry over: the coherent joint transmission technique introduces cross terms in the powers that destroy the block-concavity on which it relies. We develop a change of variables that restores block-concavity, yielding an algorithm with closed-form auxiliary updates and a concave power update, and we give a self-contained proof of non-decreasing convergence to a directional stationary point. Simulations establish two facts: first, percentile optimization retains its value in an architecture with no cell edges; relative to the weighted minimum mean-square error benchmark, it raises the average rate of the lowest-10th-percentile UEs by 56--72% and Jain's fairness index from below 0.92 to above 0.99. Second, compared directly with massive MIMO and small cells under the same SLqP utility, UC-mMIMO delivers the highest lower-percentile rates at every access point density tested, by up to 62% and 2.7$\times$ respectively, at the same fairness, and its advantage widens with densification.
item.dc:creator: Ahmad Khan, Hussein A. Ammar, Raviraj Adve

item.title: BE-CTDE: Blockchain-Enabled Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Anomaly Detection and Token Economics
item.description: arXiv:2610.34121v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning supports cooperative decision-making in Internet of Things systems, but strategic deviations can disrupt coordination and undermine confidence in the training process. This paper proposes Blockchain-Enabled Centralized Training and Decentralized Execution (BE-CTDE), which uses blockchain as an active training-management layer. A behavioral verifier compares executed trajectories with shared-policy recommendations; its flags drive a token mechanism combining slashing, burning, rewards, and compensation. Retained balances determine each agent's contribution to the global policy update, connecting auditable behavior to learning influence. We derive a one-round incentive condition that accounts for action-dependent compensation and the payoff from deviation, and a finite expected exclusion-time bound under explicit conditional detection and accounting assumptions, showing perfect detection is unnecessary. An exact finite-population capacity bound characterizes the limits of the population-relative detector. In multi-agent path finding experiments, BE-CTDE outperforms a state-of-the-art learning-based path planner with substantially higher success rates under attack, even when adversaries form the majority. It also outperforms partially defended baselines in all configurations, with collision rates up to 35% lower than under detection without economic consequences and up to 43% lower than under conventional stake slashing. Together, these results characterize how behavioral verification and token feedback can support accountable cooperative learning.
item.dc:creator: Chih-Wei Huang, Hsin-Chieh Lee, Yun-Chen Yu, Ibrahim Althamary, Rongxing Lu, Phone Lin

item.title: Networked Humanoid Intelligence: Communication, Coordination, Collaboration, and Social Interaction
item.description: arXiv:2610.34740v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Humanoid robots are moving from laboratory platforms toward connected fleets that share workspaces, infrastructure, tasks, and knowledge with other robots and humans. As deployments grow, the operation and improvement of each humanoid depend on information exchanged across the network. However, existing research has largely studied humanoids as individual systems. This survey examines networked humanoid intelligence through four functions of information exchange: communication, coordination, collaboration, and social intelligence with human interaction. We first establish the foundations of networked humanoid systems, define the question addressed by each function, and connect them through a common factory scenario. We review the literature along six dimensions: interaction architecture, exchanged information, physical coupling, operating timescale, system scale, and embodiment. We separate results obtained with physical and simulated humanoids from those based on other robotic platforms or disembodied agents, because the latter do not fully capture humanoid-specific constraints such as balance, whole-body motion, contact, and physical interaction. We examine hardware, datasets, and benchmarks, and distinguish risks handled locally from those networking introduces, such as stale information or unsafe knowledge propagation. Finally, we identify open problems in control-aware networking, compact body-centric messages, physically grounded coordination, network- and embodiment-aware knowledge sharing, fleet-level social consistency, and accountable human oversight.
item.dc:creator: Loc X. Nguyen, Huy Q. Le, Ji Su Yoon, Nguyen H. Tran, Eui-Nam Huh, Choong Seon Hong

item.title: HiLO: Towards Product-Level Graceful Degradation with a Quality-Aware, Load-Aware Control Framework
item.description: arXiv:2610.34844v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Graceful degradation is a key mechanism employed by large-scale systems to handle overload conditions. Its importance has grown further as GPU-intensive LLM inference introduces persistent capacity constraints that cannot be addressed through provisioning alone. Common degradation approaches rely on service-level mechanisms such as load shedding and circuit breakers, or on feature-level switches (some manually controlled) to preserve availability and quality. While effective at protecting services, such approaches lead to untestable product states and thereby unpredictable product quality. We present HiLO (High Load Optimizer), an automated product-level degradation system designed to handle graceful degradation at scale. HiLO maps observed load to a product state lattice: a small set of pre-validated product states, partially ordered by degradation severity. Dependencies are resolved at design time enabling deterministic and continuous control without requiring runtime dependency discovery. The same abstraction applies unchanged across heterogeneous services, including GPU-intensive deep models, LLMs and their serving layers. At Microsoft, HiLO is deployed in Bing (serving over a billion monthly active users), where it manages on average two traffic surges per week across all datacenters, bounding OneDCG (relevance) drop to under 0.5 points (the operational target) even under sustained load exceeding 2$\times$ baseline peak. HiLO complements existing service-level protections with product-level coordination and makes product quality measurable, testable and predictable.
item.dc:creator: Knut Magne Risvik, Zhuowei Li, Nirupam Purushothama, Hunter Su, Greg Dunham, Yan Reznikov

item.title: Efficient Exact Unlearning for Federated Zeroth-Order Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.35211v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Federated zeroth-order optimization (FedZOO) reduces the memory and communication costs of collaborative training for edge intelligence by avoiding backpropagation while communicating only random seeds and scalar coefficients. However, existing methods lack efficient mechanisms for exact unlearning to fully remove the influence of training data when users request deletion. A key insight is that total variation stability of the learning algorithm creates overlap between model distributions before and after data deletion, allowing exact unlearning to reuse computation through coupling. Based on this observation, we jointly design two stable zeroth-order learning algorithms and their corresponding exact-unlearning procedures: \textsc{FedZOO-S} obtains stability through client and mini-batch subsampling, enabling \textsc{FedZOUL-S} to perform efficient unlearning by preserving earlier updates and restarting from the first affected step. \textsc{FedZOO-NS} further combines subsampling with Gaussian noise to increase overlap between update distributions; \textsc{FedZOUL-NS} exploits this overlap through rejection--reflection coupling to reuse affected updates when the coupling is accepted. We prove exact unlearning for both algorithms: the model and saved state have the same joint distribution as retraining with the corresponding learner on retained data. We further establish stability and convergence guarantees for the learning algorithms and derive upper bounds on expected unlearning cost. Experiments demonstrate effective unlearning with competitive model utility and up to $56.1\%$ less cumulative unlearning time than re-optimization. Compared with first-order baselines, our methods reduce communication overhead by up to approximately four orders of magnitude.
item.dc:creator: Weijun Yin, Yanqing Yao, Falko Dressler, Di Wang, Youming Tao

item.title: One-Shot Federated Model Editing for Device Dynamics at the Edge
item.description: arXiv:2610.35212v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Standard federated learning (FL) requires persistent device connectivity across multiple communication rounds, making it unsuitable for dynamic environments such as vehicular networks, where devices frequently join and leave. One-shot FL offers a promising alternative by completing training in a single communication round. However, one-shot FL suffers from model solidification and cannot readily adapt to subsequent client dynamics, including new client contributions and the withdrawal of previous contributions. We therefore consider exact model editing, which removes withdrawn contributions through unlearning or incorporates newly contributed ones through incremental learning without retraining from scratch. We identify that efficient editing fundamentally hinges on learning stability. To this end, we propose F-SOSA, the first stable one-shot FL algorithm that enables rapid and exact model editing. F-SOSA leverages sub-sampling of local models with carefully tuned rate for stable aggregation and performs curvature-aware model fusion to preserve utility. We prove that F-SOSA achieves vanishing training error and reasonably small generalization error bounds. Building on this stability, we further develop two single-round editing algorithms: F-SOSA-U for unlearning and F-SOSA-I for incremental learning. They ensure that the edited model, along with all intermediate algorithmic states, is statistically indistinguishable from retraining while incurring only an expected $O(\rho)$ fraction of its cost, where $\rho$ quantifies stability. Experiments demonstrate that our approach matches retraining performance while reducing cumulative time and communication overhead by at least 36% and 22%, respectively, under realistic urban mobility simulations.
item.dc:creator: Youming Tao, Weijun Yin, Huanyi Xie, Yanqing Yao, Dongxiao Yu, Xiuzhen Cheng, Di Wang, Falko Dressler

item.title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking
item.description: arXiv:2610.35591v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Edge-centric IoT systems are increasingly evaluated through sensor values or platform features, yet the telemetry pipeline itself, the sequence of sensing, serialization, message mediation, ingestion, and persistence, is rarely released as a measurable object. This limits reproducible benchmarking of timeliness, provenance, and operational cost, especially in early-stage IoT design where real deployments and high-quality open data are often unavailable. I present a measurement-first edge IoT testbed and dataset that elevate timeliness, provenance, and energy to first-class telemetry dimensions. The testbed operationalizes a role-based event-driven architecture with explicit Source-Broker-Aggregator responsibilities and a schema-governed TelemetryMessage envelope (Avro) that embeds correlation identifiers and a uniform, cross-role vocabulary of stage-level timestamps. To trace mediation effects, I extend an MQTT broker (Eclipse Mosquitto) with a plugin that annotates messages with high-precision ingress/egress timestamps. I release the dataset in a dual representation: (i) replayable raw events as compressed Avro streams and (ii) analysis-ready long-format Parquet tables partitioned for efficient query and benchmarking, generated by a deterministic raw-to-tabular transformation pipeline. The contribution is an integrated engineering artifact and dataset built from established components. The demonstration describes one deployment through latency summaries, measurement-context distributions, and energy aggregates; it does not establish a new attribution method or a controlled performance benchmark. By co-releasing heterogeneous telemetry with pipeline timing and energy signals in both replayable and queryable forms, the artifact provides a basis for reproducible exploratory analysis and subsequent benchmarking studies.
item.dc:creator: Dimitris Gkoulis

item.title: Information-Theoretic Secure Aggregation With Heterogeneous Client Quantization
item.description: arXiv:2610.35833v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In federated learning (FL), secure aggregation enables a server to compute the sum of local model updates of $N$ clients, without revealing any information on the individual model updates to the server, beyond their sum. Different clients may be subject to heterogeneous bandwidth constraints, and consequently may choose different numbers of quantization levels to represent the information they send. Most secure aggregation works require the clients to project the values of their update parameters to a common finite group (or field), which does not directly accommodate heterogeneous precision constraints on their transmitted masked updates. Existing approaches of secure aggregation with heterogeneous quantization levels reveal partial aggregates of model-updates, and can reveal segments of individual model updates, under certain dropout and client-server collusion patterns. To prevent this privacy breach, we propose an information-theoretic secure aggregation scheme that tolerates client drop-outs, and up to $T$ semi-honest clients that collude with each other and with the server, under heterogeneous quantization at clients. Our protocol utilizes the $(T+1, N)$ threshold black-box secret sharing construction, where secret shares of the client updates, despite belonging to distinct algebraic groups owing to different quantization, are generated from identical linear integer systems.
item.dc:creator: Shreya Meel, Sennur Ulukus, Itzhak Tamo

item.title: Smart-TCP: An Agentic AI-based Autonomous and Adaptive TCP Protocol
item.description: arXiv:2512.00491v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) relies on deterministic state machines and sequence-number arithmetic to ensure reliable communication. However, hard-coded protocol logic is difficult to adapt to increasingly complex and dynamic network conditions. This paper proposes Smart-TCP, an agentic AI-based transport protocol framework that organizes TCP control logic as a fast/slow model-assisted decision process. Specifically, a feature-aware classifier routes routine segments to a lightweight Small Language Model (SLM) fast path and anomalous or boundary cases to a Large Language Model (LLM) slow path, while an Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) handles deterministic computation of sequence and acknowledgment numbers. A state module maintains connection state, packet history, and key control variables, enabling protocol decisions over the full session context. A scoped Protocol Guard checks candidate decisions against RFC-derived rules before execution. We evaluate Smart-TCP through path classification, atomic packet processing, slow-path anomaly response, and end-to-end session interaction. Experimental results show that Smart-TCP achieves 99.14% action accuracy on 700 slow-path anomaly and fallback samples, and a 100% full-lifecycle success rate over 300 ideal fast-path end-to-end session windows. The ordinary 32-KiB transfer tests achieve a 96.5% completion rate at 20% segment loss. These results suggest that separating model-based protocol decisions from deterministic arithmetic improves the reliability of TCP control for network service operation.
item.dc:creator: Yule Han, Kezhi Wang, Yizhe Zhao, Kun Yang

item.title: Fidelity-Guaranteed Entanglement Routing with Distributed Purification Planning
item.description: arXiv:2605.00246v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many quantum-network applications require end-to-end Bell pairs whose fidelity exceeds a request-specific threshold, but existing entanglement routing algorithms either optimize only throughput without regard for fidelity or enforce fidelity guarantees using centralized controllers with global link-state knowledge. We present Q-GUARD, an online entanglement routing algorithm that enforces per-request fidelity thresholds within a distributed protocol model in which nodes exchange link-state information only with their $k$-hop neighbors. After link outcomes are realized in each slot, Q-GUARD builds per-link purification cost tables from realized Bell pairs, allocates per-hop fidelity targets using a Werner-state equal-split rule, and selects between candidate path segments using a segment-local expected-goodput (EXG) metric that jointly accounts for swap success, purification overhead, and resource availability. We also introduce Q-GUARD-WS, an extension that exploits per-link hardware quality estimates to allocate purification effort non-uniformly across hops. On synthetic 100-node topologies with heterogeneous link fidelity and stochastic BBPSSW purification, Q-GUARD raises the qualified success rate from under 20\% to over 85\% on 4-hop paths and nearly doubles the qualified service radius in Euclidean distance relative to throughput-only and naive-purification baselines, while Q-GUARD-WS provides additional throughput gains under high hardware heterogeneity.
item.dc:creator: Anthony Gatti, Anoosha Fayyaz, Prashant Krishnamurthy, Kaushik P. Seshadreesan, Amy Babay

item.title: Can We Trust AI in 6G? Verifiable and Auditable AI-Driven Trustworthy Wireless Networks
item.description: arXiv:2607.26409v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mobile network operators are increasingly exploring the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to automate network tasks such as cell selection and mobility management. Current assurance methods for these AI functions are forms of output testing. They check what a function decides, but they cannot show why it decided that way, and two functions can pass the same tests for different reasons. In this paper, we propose mechanistic auditing, which inspects the internal features of an AI function and checks them against machine-verifiable 3GPP specifications. We set out a three-step auditing principle that locates protocol-relevant features, verifies whether decisions depend on them, and audits each decision against them. We then present an audit-native network architecture. In this architecture, a dedicated verification agent certifies each AI function before deployment and audits its decisions during operation. In a case study on a language model for LTE signalling, we find internal features that carry the 3GPP handover concepts. Removing them lowers the model's accuracy on handover tasks from 96% to 0%, while removing the same number of random features changes its accuracy by less than two points. An audit of a handover decision can therefore check whether these features are active when the model makes that decision. We also discuss the open challenges that remain before mechanistic auditing can enter telecommunications practice and standardisation.
item.dc:creator: Genze Jiang, Yizhou Huang, Kezhi Wang

item.title: SmartBAN on Silicon by Structured Behavioral Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2608.29036v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Wireless body area networks (WBANs) underpin the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT). IEC/ETSI SmartBAN defines a lightweight time-division multiple access (TDMA) protocol, yet published implementations on commercial hardware remain partial. The standard specifies frame formats but leaves device-internal behavior in phase control, connection lifecycle, and slot timing unspecified. We present an operational SmartBAN realization on a commercial wireless system-on-chip (Nordic nRF54L15, Arm Cortex-M33, Zephyr RTOS) that implements initial connection, scheduled uplink, and timeout-based disconnection detection through a four-layer software architecture whose hardware abstraction layer is the intended portability boundary. Hub and Node Mealy automata supply one concrete design for the unspecified phase control and connection lifecycle, as a blueprint for the firmware's event-driven dispatch. Validation with 16 concurrent Nodes over 25 hours shows conformance across every transition the build exercises (all but one), >99.99% packet delivery, and timeout-triggered reconnection after the single observed disconnection. An analytical current model fits the measurements once it uses measured state currents; with datasheet currents it underestimates the average, mostly in the radio-off state, whose current we attribute to implementation-level overhead rather than the hardware. A same-SoC comparison with Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) shows how each protocol departs from its schedule: SmartBAN, configured to send a fresh sample every interval instead of retransmitting, kept each Node's frame spacing within 1.1 ms of the interval but lost some frames; BLE lost none but deferred some by one or two intervals, and drew less than half SmartBAN's average current.
item.dc:creator: Masato Yoshimi, Takahiro Ito, Kento Tanaka, Hirokazu Tanaka

item.title: Mobile Backscatter Communication for the Battery-less Internet of Things
item.description: arXiv:2609.01465v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We enable backscatter communication in the battery-less mobile Internet of Things (IoT). Backscatter communication is extensively studied in static settings. Existing designs are, however, fundamentally mismatched with mobility and time-varying energy patterns. Channel conditions rapidly fluctuate, impacting the achievable data rates and thus transmission costs. Energy availability varies unpredictably, possibly forcing devices to remain quiescent to recharge energy buffers. The two issues compound each other: while recharging, a battery-less mobile IoT device may miss more favorable channel conditions. We design a lightweight decision system that dynamically determines when to transmit by checking short-term trends in signal strength, while using Non-volatile Memory (NVM) to retain packets in unfavorable channel conditions and across energy failures. Using a prototype we built and real-world mobility and power traces, we compare our design against a rate-adaptive baseline that only considers the instantaneous channel conditions. Experimental results show that our system improves throughput by up to 5.16x while reducing transmission energy consumption by up to 47.3%, with only 0.23% - 7.3% additional energy overhead.
item.dc:creator: Weining Song, Thiemo Voigt, Stefanos Kaxiras, Yuan Yao, Luca Mottola

item.title: Efficient Co-simulator Integration with Application to Smart Grids
item.description: arXiv:2609.03118v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The evolution of the electric power grid towards a ``smart grid'' is an example of an emerging large-scale cyber-physical system. To study the potential of cyberattacks or other sources of extreme events, high-fidelity co-simulation is one of the few realistic strategies. In this work, we demonstrate a practical and high-performance co-simulation strategy for smart grids, which provides lessons about co-simulation integration that can be carried over to other cyber-physical systems. Specifically, we present a co-simulation platform based on the Mosaik framework that integrates several federates including OpenDSS for power flow, a refined NS-3 for communication networks, and custom Python-based simulators for on-load tap changer control, distributed state estimation, and data collection. We compare synchronization strategies -- exhaustive lock-step time advancement versus an optimized event-driven approach that exploits lower-bound time stamps (LBTS) and next-event prediction -- and introduce targeted refinements to NS-3 event handling and relevance filtering of internal events. Performance is evaluated on two standard IEEE benchmark systems: the 13-node test feeder with tap-changer voltage regulation and a large-scale 33-bus system augmented with 32 European low-voltage feeders (1,793 nodes total) performing distributed state estimation with thousands of phasors and smart meters. Experimental results demonstrate that the refined event-based synchronization that uses LBTS-based NS-3 event filtering reduces execution time by up to 50\% over non-filtered LBTS, and more than 4$\times$ in the tap control scenario compared to na\"ive lock-step methods, while strictly preserving temporal correctness and simulation accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Talha Ibn Aziz, Jihoon Og, Ioanis Nikolaidis, Omid Ardakanian

item.title: Movable Antennas Enabled Wireless Powered Networks: Principles and Technologies
item.description: arXiv:2609.08042v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As an emerging framework, movable antenna (MA)-enabled wireless powered networks (WPNs) have attracted growing attention. WPNs integrate wireless communication and energy transfer. MA can dynamically adjust the position of antenna units by introducing additional spatial degrees of freedom, so as to make full use of channel gain, optimize the effect of energy beamforming, and further improve the performance of WPNs. In this article, we first classify the implementations of MA by driving architectures, and review the fundamental principles of WPNs. We then highlight the key advantages of MA-enabled WPNs in enhancing wireless power transfer efficiency, realizing flexible and adaptive beamforming, and improving system robustness and interference resilience. Furthermore, four representative application scenarios and three key enabling technologies are discussed. A case study is also presented to show the reduction in transmit power brought by MA for WPNs. Finally, we discuss the challenges and future directions of MA-enabled WPNs, aiming to provide reference for future research and practice.
item.dc:creator: Zhendong Li, Yiran Zheng, Tianyu Li, Zhou Su, Wen Chen, Ying Wang

item.title: Prefix Visibility Ratio: Quantifying Partial Observability in Carpet Bombing Detection
item.description: arXiv:2610.29802v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Carpet bombing attacks distribute malicious traffic across many destinations within a network prefix, while operational monitoring commonly provides destination-specific telemetry for only a subset of those targets. This creates an attack-conditional observability problem that is not captured by address utilization or nominal monitoring coverage. We introduce the Prefix Visibility Ratio (PVR), defined as the fraction of attacked destinations for which the telemetry required by the host-level evidence plane is available, and argue that PVR should be treated as an explicit evaluation dimension for carpet bombing detection. We then present VANTA (Visibility-Aware Network Threat Analysis) as one concrete way to operationalize this principle. VANTA combines host-level and prefix-level anomaly scores, estimates PVR online from router-side destination evidence and the monitored-destination inventory, and adjusts evidence fusion according to both estimated visibility and estimator confidence. Across a validated campaign of 2,160 Mininet runs, VANTA achieves 99.18% precision, 93.46% recall, a global F1-score of 96.24%, and a 1.54% false-positive rate. In a separate matched-observability study using task-adapted feature-level reference implementations, VANTA reaches 95.89% pooled F1 and 92.39% recall for configured PVR<=10%, with its largest advantage appearing at configured PVR=1%. These reference comparisons are intended to isolate observability effects under a common binary detection task rather than to reproduce the original end-to-end objectives of the referenced systems. The results establish attacked-destination visibility as a measurable factor that can materially change detector behavior and should be reported explicitly in future carpet bombing evaluations.
item.dc:creator: Farid Na\"it-Abdesselam, Laaziz Lahlou, Doha Bentaoussy, Hugo Lege, Eve Lin, Nadjia Kara

item.title: Building Automotive Security on Internet Standards: In-Car Service Authentication with DNSSEC, DANE, and DANCE
item.description: arXiv:2506.13261v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The automotive industry trends to softwarizing cars according to flexible, service-oriented architectures. At the same time, connected cars become networked computer systems but lack proper security measures. In this paper, we propose to authenticate and authorize in-vehicle services by integrating DNSSEC, DANE, and DANCE with automotive middleware. Our approach decouples the cryptographic authentication of the service from that of the service deployment with the help of DNSSEC and thereby largely simplifies key management. We propose to authenticate in-vehicle services by certificates that are solely generated by the service suppliers but published on deployment via DNSSEC TLSA records solely signed by the OEM. We further show how these established Internet standards secure the service discovery and invocation, ensure interoperability with various protocols, and scale management of credentials for millions of connected vehicles at robust security levels. We back our design proposal by a security analysis using the STRIDE threat model and by evaluations in an emulation of a realistic in-vehicle setup that demonstrate its effectiveness.
item.dc:creator: Timo Salomon, Mehmet Mueller, Philipp Meyer, Thomas C. Schmidt

item.title: Agentic AI Empowered Intent-Based Networking for 6G
item.description: arXiv:2601.06640v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The transition towards sixth-generation (6G) wireless networks necessitates autonomous orchestration mechanisms capable of translating high-level operational intents into executable network configurations. Existing approaches to Intent-Based Networking (IBN) rely upon either rule-based systems that struggle with linguistic variation or end-to-end neural models that lack interpretability and fail to enforce operational constraints. This paper presents a hierarchical multi-agent framework where Large Language Model (LLM) based agents autonomously decompose natural language intents, consult domain-specific specialists, and synthesise technically feasible network slice configurations through iterative reasoning-acting (ReAct) cycles. The proposed architecture employs an orchestrator agent coordinating two specialist agents, namely Radio Access Network (RAN) and Core Network agents, via ReAct-style reasoning, grounded in structured network state representations. Experimental evaluation across diverse benchmark scenarios demonstrates that the proposed system outperforms monolithic agents, rule-based systems, and direct LLM prompting, with architectural principles applicable to Open RAN (O-RAN) deployments. The results also demonstrate that whilst contemporary LLMs possess substantial general telecommunications knowledge, structured prompt engineering encoding domain-specific decision thresholds and operational policies is essential for reliable network automation performance.
item.dc:creator: Genze Jiang, Kezhi Wang, Xiaomin Chen, Yizhou Huang

item.title: A Density--Delay Law for Event-Driven State Progression in Open Distributed Systems
item.description: arXiv:2603.26758v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper studies delay-induced competition in an honest event-driven longest-chain network and distinguishes selected-tip divergence from lowest-common-ancestor (LCA) competing-branch depth. With density--delay load \(x_N=\lambda\Delta_{\max}\), regenerative analysis gives the explicit network-size-uniform bound \(\mu_N(x_N)\le e^{2x_N}+e^{x_N}-2\) on proposal-clock mean LCA depth. Bounded \(x_N\) suffices for this guarantee. At fixed delay, \(g(N)=O(1/N)\) is one corresponding input-rate scaling. An explicit finite-horizon depth-exceedance bound is also established. Explicit-node simulations show strong load effects and comparatively small finite-size effects. The results concern honest contention, not adversarial security.
item.dc:creator: Bin Chen, Dechuang Huang

item.title: Agentic Societies Need a Social Harness
item.description: arXiv:2609.17527v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: An agentic society is a collection of AI agents that coordinate autonomously across trust boundaries on behalf of different principals. We show experimentally that in such societies even honest, competent agents often fail to reach satisfactory outcomes when using current harnesses and messaging primitives; and faulty or malicious agents can completely stall progress, influence outcomes, and pursue harmful goals by exploiting communication vulnerabilities. We argue that agentic societies need a \emph{social harness}. Unlike a \emph{personal harness}, which manages private context and communication with the principal, a social harness manages interactions with other agents. We propose a layered architecture for social harnesses which (i) prevents classes of communication failures outright, (ii) enables agents to detect invalid messages, and (iii) supports post-facto investigation and consequences.
item.dc:creator: Tapan Chugh, Vidushi Singh, Krish Jain, Arvind Krishnamurthy, Ratul Mahajan

item.title: VX-One: Typed, Calibrated Decision Heads for Real-Time Perimeter Triage
item.description: arXiv:2610.30090v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Perimeter triage faces a latency/semantics trade-off: signature engines are fast and format-safe but blind to unseen attacks, while generative models are semantic but slow and unparseable. We present VX-One, a small multi-head network (100K--10M parameters) with calibrated typed outputs: a binary gate, a closed-set choice with an explicit unknown option where the benchmark supports it (and abstention elsewhere), and an ordinal score. Heads are temperature-calibrated, with 0.7--1.7 ms single-event CPU p50 latency. We evaluate UNSW-NB15, CIC-IDS2017, and EMBER2024 against calibrated XGBoost, Random Forest, MLP, and Kitsune baselines, and measure a Suricata-to-VX-One cascade over five days of CIC-IDS2017. Results are deliberately double-sided: on UNSW the gate ties the best baseline (0.9837+/-0.0002 versus MLP 0.9835+/-0.0013 across three seeds), while VX-One wins temporal CIC detection (0.734+/-0.022 versus 0.639+/-0.027) but loses multi-class attribution to XGBoost. Under leave-one-family-out, the gate detects all nine UNSW families but drops below chance on CIC recon; CIC trees transfer better. Suricata resolves only about 0.1% of attacks on flow reconstructions and 0.2--2.2% on payload-bearing PCAPs; the strictly by-day Phase 2 recovers only the in-scope DoS/DDoS share on the wave day (recall 0.34, precision 0.97). Calibration collapses under temporal drift (ECE 0.04->0.40) for every method while ranking partly survives. We contribute a measured account of where typed calibrated decisions help perimeter triage, and where they fail.
item.dc:creator: Juan S. Santillana
